title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Camp before Alcocer; the town taken by a feigned retreat (tiradas 27–31, lines 557–622)
part: Tiradas 27–31 · Camp before Alcocer; the town taken by a feigned retreat (lines 557–622)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 162–166, lines 557–622 (tiradas 27–31). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Bien puebla el otero, firme prende las posadas,
los unos contra la sierra e los otros contra la agua.
sentences.l:
Well he-settles the hill, firmly he-takes the lodgings,
the ones toward the sierra and the others toward the water.
sentences.i: He settles the hill well and pitches his camp firmly, some of his men facing the sierra and some the water.
sentences.n: Tirada 27 (assonance á-a) — the Çid camps before Alcocer (Pidal's rubric: El Cid acampa sobre Alcocer). The endings run posadas, agua, espada, agua, cárcava, arrebata, fincança: stressed á, then a. poblar, 'to settle, occupy': the Çid treats the hill as a settlement, not a halt. prender = 'to take' (modern prender is chiefly 'to seize, arrest'); prender posadas, 'to take up quarters, pitch camp'. contra = 'toward, facing', not 'against'. la agua: modern el agua was not yet fixed.

sentences.t:
El buen Canpeador que en buen ora [cinxo espada]
derredor del otero, bien çerca del agua,
a todos sos varones mandó fazer una cárcava,
sentences.l:
The good Canpeador who in good hour [girded sword]
around of-the hill, well near of-the water,
to all his barons ordered to-make a ditch,
sentences.i: The good Campeador, who in a good hour girded on his sword, ordered all his barons to dig a trench round the hill, close down to the water,
sentences.n: The en buen ora formula, in its sword-girding form. cinxo espada (cinxo, strong preterite of çeñir, 'girded') is printed in italics by Pidal, that is, supplied by him; the á-a assonance needs a word like espada at the line-end. Canpeador, with n before p, is the scribe's spelling, kept beside Campeador. derredor, 'around'. varones, 'barons, men of rank', here simply his fighting men. mandó fazer, 'ordered to be made'; fazer = hacer (Latin f- kept where modern Spanish has h-). cárcava, 'ditch, trench': Pidal notes that the Çid makes a camp with a ditch as much for defence as to frighten the Moors, announcing that he means to stay.

sentences.t:
que de día nin de noch non les diessen arrebata,
que sopiessen que mio Çid allí avie fincança.
sentences.l:
that by day nor by night not to-them they-should-give surprise,
that they-should-know that my Çid there had staying.
sentences.i: so that no one could fall on them by surprise, by day or by night, and so that all should know that my Çid had come there to stay.
sentences.n: que … que: the first que is 'so that' (purpose, with the subjunctive diessen, from dar), the second adds a further aim. nin … non: the Old Spanish double negative. noch = noche, cut. arrebata, 'a sudden attack, a surprise' (cf. arrebatar, 'to snatch'); the subject of diessen is an unnamed enemy. sopiessen, imperfect subjunctive of saber. avie fincança: fincança, from fincar 'to remain' (f- again; modern hincar), is 'staying, permanence'. Pidal: the ditch announced the Çid's permanence, his fincança, in the country.

sentences.t:
Por todas essas tierras ivan los mandados,
que el Campeador mio Çid allí avie poblado,
venido es a moros, exido es de cristianos;
en la su vezindad non se treven ganar tanto.
sentences.l:
Through all those lands went the tidings,
that the Campeador my Çid there had settled,
come he-is to Moors, gone-out he-is from Christians;
in the his neighbourhood not themselves they-dare to-till much.
sentences.i: Through all those lands the news went out that the Campeador, my Çid, had settled there: he had come among the Moors, he had left the Christians behind; with him for a neighbour they scarcely dare to work their fields.
sentences.n: Tirada 28 (assonance á-o) — fear among the Moors (Pidal: Temor de los moros). mandados, 'messages, tidings'. avie poblado, 'had settled' (poblar again, v. 557). venido es, exido es: verbs of motion take ser, not aver, as the perfect auxiliary ('is come, is gone out'); exido from exir, 'to go out'. a moros … de cristianos: into Moorish land, away from Christian land. la su vezindad, article + possessive, 'his neighbourhood'. treven = (se) atreven, 'dare'. ganar: Pidal argues that it must mean 'to till the land' here, like Old French gaignier (compare modern gañán, 'farmhand'): 'because of the Çid's presence the Moors scarcely dare to work their holdings'. He offers it as what 'the sense must be', so the reading is likely but not certain; tanto, 'so much', softens it to 'scarcely'.

sentences.t:
[Alegr]ando se va mio Çid con todos s[o]s vassallos;
el castiello de Alcoçer en paria va entrando.
sentences.l:
[Rejoic]ing himself goes my Çid with all his vassals;
the castle of Alcoçer into tribute goes entering.
sentences.i: My Çid goes rejoicing with all his vassals; the castle of Alcocer comes under tribute to him.
sentences.n: [Alegr]ando and s[o]s: letters printed in italics by Pidal, that is, supplied by him (sos is the regular 'his'). alegrarse, 'to rejoice'; se va … alegrando, ir + gerund. paria (usually plural parias), the tribute a Moorish town paid a Christian lord to be left in peace. Pidal notes that ir + gerund often has no special durative force: en paria va entrando means only 'enters into tribute', that is, 'pays tribute', as the linking line that opens the next tirada repeats (v. 570).

sentences.i: The men of Alcocer now pay my Çid tribute, and so do those of Ateca and the town of Terrer; to those of Calatayud, mark this, it was a heavy grief.
sentences.n: Tirada 29 (assonance á-a) — the Campeador takes Alcocer by a stratagem (Pidal: El Campeador toma a Alcocer mediante un ardid). The first line takes up the last of the previous tirada (en paria va entrando, v. 569). yal = ya le, 'already to him'. Teca is Ateca (as v. 552); Pidal: Ateca and Terrer are two villages on the Jalón 7 km apart, and the vanished castle of Alcocer stood between them. Ter[rer]: the last syllable is Pidal's. la casa: probably 'the town, the stronghold' of Terrer; the word order (los de Terrer la casa) is odd and the exact sense is not certain. Calatauth is Calatayud, 6 km from Terrer (Pidal). sabet, 'know ye' (imperative of saber, -t for -d): the minstrel's aside to his audience. ma'les: Pidal notes ma' les for mal les, 'ill to them'; pesar, 'to grieve, weigh on'.

sentences.t: Allí yogo mio Çid complidas quinze se[d]manas.
sentences.l: There lay my Çid full fifteen weeks.
sentences.i: There my Çid lay encamped for fifteen full weeks.
sentences.n: yogo, strong preterite of yazer (modern yacer), 'lay, stayed', as an army lies before a town. complidas = cumplidas, 'complete, full'. se[d]manas = semanas: the d is supplied by Pidal; sedmana is the older form, from Latin septimana.

sentences.t:
Quando vi[d]o mio Çid que Alcoçer non se le dava,
el[le] fizo un art e non lo detardava:
sentences.l:
When saw my Çid that Alcoçer not itself to-him gave,
he made a trick and not it delayed:
sentences.i: When my Çid saw that Alcocer would not surrender to him, he devised a stratagem and lost no time about it:
sentences.n: vi[d]o = vio, 'saw', the older form with -d-, the d supplied by Pidal. non se le dava, 'would not give itself up to him': darse, 'to surrender'. el[le]: elle, an old form of él 'he', the le supplied by Pidal. art, 'a stratagem of war' (Pidal), the same word as arte. detardar, 'to delay'. Note the tenses: fizo (preterite) beside detardava (imperfect); the poem mixes tenses freely, for vividness and for the assonance.

sentences.t:
dexa una tienda fita e las otras levava,
cojó’ Salón ayuso, la su seña alçada,
las lorigas vestidas e çintas las espadas,
a guisa de menbrado, por sacarlos a çelada.
sentences.l:
he-leaves one tent pitched and the others he-took-away,
he-took-himself Salón down, the his banner raised,
the hauberks put-on and girded the swords,
in manner of prudent-man, to draw-them into ambush.
sentences.i: he leaves one tent standing and carries off the rest, and makes his way down the Jalón with his banner raised, his men in their mail and their swords girded on, like a shrewd captain, to draw them out into an ambush.
sentences.n: dexa … levava: present beside imperfect, the same tense-mixing. fita, 'fixed, pitched' (past participle; cf. modern hito, 'landmark'). cojó' Salón ayuso: Pidal explains cojó' as cogióse, 'went off down the Jalón' ; the reflexive s is apparently lost before the S- of Salón (the apostrophe marks the cut; compare cojós, v. 589). ayuso, 'down, downstream'. la su seña, article + possessive. lorigas, 'hauberks, mail coats'. vestidas … çintas: participles agreeing with their nouns, 'the hauberks donned, the swords girded'; çintas is the old participle of çeñir (cf. cinxo, v. 559). menbrado, 'prudent, mindful' (from membrar, 'to remember'). sacarlos a çelada, 'to draw them out into an ambush'.

sentences.t: V[id]ienlo los de Alcoçer, Dios, cómmo se alabavan!
sentences.l: They-saw-him those of Alcoçer, God, how themselves they-praised!
sentences.i: The men of Alcocer saw him go — God, how they crowed!
sentences.n: V[id]ienlo = veíanlo, 'they saw him': vidien is an old imperfect of ver; the id is Pidal's. alabarse, 'to boast, glory'. The narrator's exclamation Dios, … is a stock epic device.

sentences.t:
“Fallido [ha] a mio Çid el pan e la çevada.
Las otras abés lieva, una tienda a dexada.
sentences.l:
“Failed [has] to my Çid the bread and the barley.
The others scarcely he-carries, one tent he-has left.
sentences.i: “My Çid has run out of bread and barley. He can barely carry off the other tents — one he has left behind.
sentences.n: The townsmen's speech runs to v. 586. Fallido [ha] a mio Çid …: fallir a uno, 'to fail someone, run short' ('the bread has failed him'); ha is supplied by Pidal. çevada, 'barley', fodder for the horses. abés = apenas; Pidal: 'he carries the other tents with difficulty'. a dexada = ha dexada: the participle agrees with its object (una tienda … dexada), as often in Old Spanish, and the h of the auxiliary is not written.

sentences.t:
De guisa va mio Çid commo si escapasse de arrancada;
demos salto a él e feremos grant ganançia,
sentences.l:
In manner goes my Çid as if he-escaped from rout;
let-us-give leap at him and we-shall-make great gain,
sentences.i: My Çid is going like a man fleeing a defeat; let us fall on him and we will win great spoil,
sentences.n: De guisa … commo si, 'in such a way as if'. arrancada, 'defeat, rout' (Pidal). escapasse, imperfect subjunctive of escapar. demos salto a él, 'let us make a sally at him'. feremos, future of fazer, 'we shall make' (= haremos; f- again). ganançia, 'gain, booty'.

sentences.i: before the men of Terrer can take him — for if they take him, they will give us nothing of it; and the tribute he has had from us he will pay back twice over.”
sentences.n: quel = que le; prendan, present subjunctive after antes que. The bracketed words are Pidal's, printed in italics: [la casa] repeats v. 571's los de Terrer la casa, and [ca si ellos le prenden] supplies the first half of the next line, which he numbers 585b himself, so the traditional count is not disturbed; his footnotes here do not discuss either restoration. ca, 'for'. dent = de ende, 'of it, thereof'. la paria qu'él a presa: a = ha, presa, participle of prender agreeing with paria. tornar nos la ha, the split future: infinitive + pronouns + ending ('return-to-us-it-he-will'). doblada, 'doubled'. Greed's reckoning: catch the Çid, and Alcocer recovers its tribute twice over.

sentences.t: Salieron de Alcoçer a una priessa much estraña.
sentences.l: They-sallied from Alcoçer at a haste very strange.
sentences.i: Out of Alcocer they poured, in an astonishing rush.
sentences.n: priessa = prisa, 'haste'. much = muy, a cut form of mucho before an adjective. estraña, 'extraordinary, outlandish'.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid, quando los vio fuera, cogiós commo de arrancada;
Cojós Salón ayuso con los sos abuelta [anda].
sentences.l:
My Çid, when them he-saw outside, took-himself as from rout;
Took-himself Salón down with the his-men together [goes].
sentences.i: My Çid, when he saw them outside the walls, made off as if routed; he takes himself down the Jalón, his men all together with him.
sentences.n: cogiós, cojós = cogióse, 'took himself off' (the full form of cojó', v. 577; the enclitic se cut to s). commo de arrancada, 'as from a rout'. The second line restates the first — the poem often doubles an action this way. con los sos, 'with his men'. abuelta, 'together, mingled' (a buelta). [anda], 'goes', is printed in italics, so supplied by Pidal (without a note here), apparently for the sense and the á-a assonance; it is a conjecture.

sentences.t: Dizen los de Alcoçer: “ya se nos va la ganançia!”
sentences.l: Say those of Alcoçer: “now from-us goes the gain!”
sentences.i: The men of Alcocer cry: “Our plunder is getting away!”
sentences.n: ya se nos va, 'now it is going away from us': irse, with nos as the dative of the losers. The Çid as their ganançia echoes v. 584.

sentences.t:
Los grandes e los chicos fuera salto da[van],
al sabor del prender de lo al non pienssan nada,
abiertas dexan las puertas que ninguno non las guarda.
sentences.l:
The great and the small outside leap gave,
at the relish of-the taking of the other not they-think nothing,
open they-leave the gates that none not them guards.
sentences.i: Great and small alike rushed out; in their lust for plunder they thought of nothing else, and left the gates open with no one to guard them.
sentences.n: fuera salto da[van], 'were sallying out' (dar salto, as v. 584); the -van is Pidal's. al sabor del prender, 'in the relish of taking': sabor, 'delight, eagerness'; del prender, an infinitive used as a noun. de lo al, 'of anything else': al, 'other' (Latin aliud). non … nada, ninguno non: double negatives. que, 'so that'.

sentences.i: The good Campeador turned his face round and saw that there was a wide stretch of ground between them and the castle; he ordered the banner turned about, and they spurred hard.
sentences.n: vío, Pidal's accented preterite (= vio). entrellos = entre ellos. avié … plaça: aver used impersonally, 'there was'; Pidal glosses plaça 'space': 'there was a very great distance'. tornar la seña: to turn the standard is to turn the whole company. espolonear, 'to spur'.

sentences.t:
“¡Firidlos, cavalleros, todos sines dubdança;
con la merçed del Criador nuestra es la ganancia!”
sentences.l:
“Strike-them, knights, all without hesitation;
with the mercy of-the Creator ours is the gain!”
sentences.i: “Strike them, knights, every one of you, and have no fear! By the Creator's grace the spoil is ours!”
sentences.n: The Çid's words, though he is not named as the speaker. Firidlos = ferid + los, 'strike them' (ferir = herir, f- for h-; imperative in -d). sines dubdança, Pidal: 'without fear' (sines = sin; dubdança, 'doubt, hesitation'). merçed, 'favour, grace'. ganancia, here without the cedilla (ganançia, v. 590): Pidal's text keeps such variation.

sentences.t:
Bueltos son con ellos por medio de la llaña.
Dios, qué bueno es el gozo por aquesta mañana!
sentences.l:
Turned they-are with them through middle of the plain.
God, how good is the joy on this morning!
sentences.i: They wheeled and closed with them out in the middle of the plain. God, how great was the joy that morning!
sentences.n: Bueltos son con ellos: Pidal glosses 'revueltos van con ellos por medio de la llanura': revueltos can mean both 'turned about' and 'mingled with them' in close fighting, and either way the feigned retreat becomes the attack. bueltos, participle of bolver (modern vuelto). llaña, 'plain, level ground' (Pidal: llanura). aquesta = esta. Another exclamation from the narrator (cf. v. 580).

sentences.i: My Çid and Álvar Fáñez spurred on ahead; they have good horses, mark you, that go just as their riders wish; and so they got in between the Moors and the castle.
sentences.n: aguijar, 'to spur on'. a su guisa les andan, 'go for them at their will': the horses answer to their riders. entrellos y el castiello, 'between them and the castle' (as v. 595): the two cut off the townsmen's way back. en essora, 'then' (Pidal: entonces).

sentences.t:
Los vassallos de mio Çid sin piedad les davan,
en un poco de logar trezientos moros matan.
sentences.l:
The vassals of my Çid without pity to-them gave,
in a little of place three-hundred Moors they-kill.
sentences.i: My Çid's vassals struck at them without mercy; in a small space they killed three hundred Moors.
sentences.n: les davan, 'were giving it to them': dar with no object, 'to strike'. en un poco de logar, 'in a little space' (logar = lugar).

sentences.t:
Dando grandes alaridos los que están en la çelada,
dexando van los delant, por[a]l castiello se tornavan,
las espadas desnudas, a la puerta se paravan.
sentences.l:
Giving great war-cries those who are in the ambush,
leaving go those in-front, toward-the castle themselves they-turned,
the swords bare, at the gate themselves they-stopped.
sentences.i: With loud war-cries the men who lay in ambush leave behind the men in front of them, turn toward the castle, and take their stand at the gate with drawn swords.
sentences.n: Pidal: 'the narration is confused.' From this line he infers that the Çid, when he feigned flight, had left part of his men hidden in ambush (çelada) to cut off the retreat of the men of Alcocer (cf. v. 631), and he adds that the chronicles do not help to clear the passage up. On his reading los que están en la çelada are the Çid's hidden men; dexando van los delant, 'they go leaving those in front', probably means they pass by the Moors fighting out on the plain, but who 'those in front' are is uncertain. alaridos, 'war-cries' (a word from Arabic). por[a]l = pora + el, 'toward the' (pora = para); the a is Pidal's. pararse, 'to take one's stand'.

sentences.t:
Luego llegavan los sos, ca fecha es el arrancada.
Mio Çid gañó a Alcoçer, sabet, por esta maña.
sentences.l:
Then arrived his-men, for done is the rout.
My Çid won Alcoçer, know-ye, by this trick.
sentences.i: Then his men came up, for the rout was complete. That, mark you, is how my Çid won Alcocer: by this ruse.
sentences.n: luego, 'then, at once' (not 'later'). los sos, 'his (men)'. fecha es, 'is done' (fecha = hecha, f- again); el arrancada: arrancada is feminine, but Old Spanish often puts el (from ela) before a noun beginning in a-. gañó = ganó. maña, 'skill, trick': the minstrel closes the tirada on how the town was won.

sentences.t:
Vino Per Verm[udoz], que la seña tiene en mano,
metióla en somo en todo lo mas alto.
sentences.l:
Came Per Verm[udoz], who the banner holds in hand,
put-it on top in all the most high.
sentences.i: Per Vermudoz came up, who bears the banner in his hand, and planted it on the very top, at the highest point of all.
sentences.n: Tirada 30 (assonance á-o) — the Çid's banner flies over Alcocer (Pidal: La seña del Cid ondea sobre Alcocer). Per Verm[udoz]: Per is a short form of Pero, that is Pedro (modern Pedro Bermúdez), the bearer of the Çid's banner; -udoz is Pidal's. metióla, 'put it' (metió + la). en somo, 'on top' (Latin summum). en todo lo mas alto, 'in the very highest place' of the castle.

sentences.t:
Fabló mio Çid R[o]y Díaz, el que en buen ora fue nado:
“grado a Dios del çielo e a todos los sos santos,
ya mejoraremos posadas a dueños e a cauallos.
sentences.l:
Spoke my Çid R[o]y Díaz, he who in good hour was born:
“thanks to God of-the heaven and to all the his saints,
now we-shall-better lodgings for masters and for horses.
sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz, born in a good hour, spoke: “Thanks be to God in heaven and to all his saints, now we shall have better quarters, for riders and horses alike.
sentences.n: R[o]y = Ruy, short for Rodrigo; only the o is Pidal's. el que en buen ora fue nado, the 'born in a good hour' form of the formula; nado = nacido. grado a Dios, 'thanks to God'. mejorar posadas, 'to better our quarters': from a camp on a hill to a walled town. dueños, 'masters', the riders as against their mounts; cauallos with u for v, as Pidal prints it. The speech runs on into the next tirada (vv. 616–622) under a new assonance.

sentences.i: Hear me, Álvar Fáñez, and all you knights! In this castle we have taken great wealth; the Moors lie dead, and I see few left alive.
sentences.n: Tirada 31 (assonance é-o) — the Çid's clemency to the Moors (Pidal: Clemencia del Cid con los moros). The speech begun in v. 614 continues: the assonance changes, the speaker does not, which is why no new quotation mark opens here. Oíd a mí, 'hear me' (a mí, emphatic). aver, 'wealth, goods', the noun (modern haber, 'assets'); avemos preso, 'we have taken' (aver + participle of prender). bivos = vivos.

sentences.t:
Los moros e la[s] moras vender non los podremos,
que los descabeçemos nada non ganaremos;
sentences.l:
The Moors and the Moor-women to-sell not them we-shall-be-able,
that them we-behead nothing not we-shall-gain;
sentences.i: We cannot sell the Moors, men or women, and we would gain nothing by cutting off their heads;
sentences.n: la[s] moras: the s is Pidal's. vender non los podremos, 'we shall not be able to sell them' as captives; the poem does not say why (perhaps no market for them so deep in Moorish country, but that is a guess). que los descabeçemos, 'that we behead them' = 'if we behead them': que + subjunctive as a condition. descabeçar, 'to behead' (cabeça, 'head'). nada non: double negative.

sentences.t:
cojámoslos de dentro, ca el señorío tenemos;
posaremos en sus casas e dellos nos serviremos.”
sentences.l:
let-us-take-them within, for the lordship we-hold;
we-shall-lodge in their houses and of-them ourselves we-shall-serve.”
sentences.i: let us take them in, since the lordship is ours; we shall lodge in their houses, and they shall serve us.”
sentences.n: cojámoslos = cojamos + los, 'let us take them' (coger; the s of -mos kept before los). de dentro, 'inside' the walls. señorío, 'lordship, dominion'. servirse de, 'to make use of, be served by'. Pidal heads the tirada 'clemency': the Moors are spared, but as a subject people who keep their town and serve its new masters — mercy that pays.
